---
title: "B: Blood and blood forming organs"
description: "ATC group B for modellers: lab biomarkers as PD drivers, delayed effects from turnover and cell lifespan, and the bleeding-thrombosis trade-off."
date: "2026-02-08"
---

Drugs acting on blood itself and on the organs that make it.
Antithrombotics (B01) carry an extensive pharmacometric literature [@mueck2014rivaroxaban; @hamberg2010warfarin; @zhou2026milvexian]; the rest of the group is modelled rarely and quite differently.

In February 1933 the farmer Ed Carlson drove 190 miles to Karl Paul Link's laboratory in Madison with a dead heifer, a milk churn of her unclotted blood and mouldy sweet clover hay.
Six years later Link's group isolated dicoumarol, the parent of warfarin [@ballHistoryWarfarin2025].

| Level 2 code | Description |
| ---: | :--- |
| B01 | Antithrombotic agents |
| B02 | Antihemorrhagics |
| B03 | Antianemic preparations |
| B05 | Blood substitutes and perfusion solutions |
| B06 | Other hematological agents |

## Modelling notes

**Endpoint.**
The PD driver is typically a laboratory measure: clotting time, anti-Xa activity, factor activity, hemoglobin [@byon2019apixaban; @wong2025efanesoctocog; @chanu2020epoetin].
Clinical events are carried separately, in exposure-response or [time-to-event](/docs/modeling/tte/) analyses [@nyberg2016edoxaban; @leil2014apixaban].

**Delayed effect is the default.**
Vitamin K antagonists suppress synthesis of clotting factors [@holford1986warfarin], and irreversible antiplatelet agents outlast the drug [@jiang2015clopidogrel], so effect follows the turnover of a protein or cell pool rather than plasma concentration.
Turnover and indirect response models are the natural starting point [@dayneka1993indirect; @ooi2017joint].

**The exception worth knowing.**
Direct oral anticoagulants inhibit an existing enzyme, so their effect on clotting assays tracks concentration with little delay and direct models are what is actually fitted [@mueck2014rivaroxaban; @stangier2007dabigatran; @parasrampuria2016edoxaban].

**Benefit-risk is asymmetric.**
Exposure-response detects the bleeding limb far more reliably than the efficacy limb, which is often flat across the range studied [@nyberg2016edoxaban; @roshammar2017ticagrelor].
Covariates that raise exposure (renal function, body size, age, P-glycoprotein and CYP3A inhibitors) move bleeding first, which is why dose-reduction criteria are written in exactly those terms [@terrier2022doacpopk; @lin2025fxaage].

**Longest delays in the group.**
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents act on precursors, so hemoglobin is separated from exposure by maturation and red cell lifespan [@uehlinger1992epo; @ramakrishnan2004epo].
Lifespan models with an explicit endogenous baseline and feedback are standard [@krzyzanski2008lifespan; @olssongisleskog2007epo].

**Easy to overlook.**
Blood substitutes and perfusion solutions have their own tradition, volume kinetics, fitted to hemoglobin-derived plasma dilution [@hahn2019albumin; @balan2025gelofusine].

**Mechanistic extrapolation.**
QSP models of the coagulation network, built from literature kinetics, are well established for predicting how anticoagulants shift thrombin generation and INR, extrapolating efficacy and bleeding risk across doses [@wajimaComprehensiveModelHumoral2009; @burghausEvaluationEfficacySafety2011].
